title: Sechse kommen durch die ganze Welt
titleEn: Six Make Their Way Through the World
part: Six Make Their Way Through the World
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 71. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng/fiengen, thun/that/gethan, theilten, Thüre, Muth, todt, ward).
about: KHM 71, a soldier’s tale rather than a magic one. Paid off at the end of a war with three Heller, an old campaigner sets out to make the king pay for the insult, and gathers on the road five men with impossible gifts: one who pulls up trees, a marksman, a blower, a runner who unstraps a leg to slow himself down, and one whose hat must stay cocked over an ear or the birds freeze in the sky. Much of the pleasure is in the accumulation — each new companion is taken on with the same words. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as gieng, fieng, thun, Muth, Reichthum and rathschlagen.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Mann, der verstand allerlei Künste:
sentences.l: There was once a man who understood all sorts of arts:
sentences.n: Künste here are not the fine arts but tricks, feats, things a man knows how to do — the word governs the whole tale, in which six men each have exactly one.

sentences.t: er diente im Krieg, und hielt sich brav und tapfer, aber als der Krieg zu Ende war, bekam er den Abschied und drei Heller Zehrgeld auf den Weg.
sentences.l: he served in the war, and held himself well and brave, but when the war was at an end, he got his discharge and three Heller of eating-money for the road.
sentences.i: he had served in the war and borne himself well and bravely; but when the war was over he was given his discharge and three Heller of travelling money for the road.
sentences.n: Zehrgeld — money to live on while travelling, from zehren, to consume. A Heller was the smallest coin there was; three of them for a war is the injury the whole plot grows out of.

sentences.t: „Wart,“ sprach er, „das laß ich mir nicht gefallen, finde ich die rechten Leute, so soll mir der König noch die Schätze des ganzen Landes heraus geben.“
sentences.l: “Wait,” said he, “that I do not let please me; if I find the right people, then the king shall yet hand out to me the treasures of the whole land.”
sentences.i: “Wait,” said he. “I shall not stand for this. If I find the right men, the king shall yet give up to me the treasures of the whole land.”
sentences.n: “das lasse ich mir nicht gefallen” — I do not let that please me: the standing phrase for refusing to put up with something. finde ich die rechten Leute is a conditional made by putting the verb first, with no wenn; it happens twice more in this tale.

sentences.t: Da gieng er voll Zorn in den Wald, und sah einen darin stehen, der hatte sechs Bäume ausgerupft, als wärens Kornhalme.
sentences.l: Then he went full of anger into the forest, and saw one standing in it who had plucked up six trees as if they were stalks of corn.
sentences.i: Then he went into the forest in a rage, and saw a man standing there who had pulled up six trees as though they were stalks of grain.
sentences.n: wärens is wären es. ausrupfen is what you do to weeds or feathers — the verb makes the trees trivial before the sentence even gets to the comparison.

sentences.t: Sprach er zu ihm „willst du mein Diener sein und mit mir ziehen?“
sentences.l: Said he to him “will you be my servant and journey with me?”
sentences.n: Sprach er zu ihm — verb first, with nothing before it. This old narrative rhythm runs all through the tale and has no exact English equivalent beyond “said he.”

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete er, „aber erst will ich meiner Mutter das Wellchen Holz heimbringen,“ und nahm einen von den Bäumen, und wickelte ihn um die fünf andern, hob die Welle auf die Schulter und trug sie fort.
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered he, “but first I want to bring my mother home the little-bundle of wood,” and took one of the trees, and wound it round the five others, lifted the bundle onto his shoulder and carried it away.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he answered, “but first I must take my mother home this little bundle of firewood” — and he took one of the trees, wound it round the other five, lifted the faggot onto his shoulder and carried it off.
sentences.n: A Welle is a faggot, brushwood bound up for the fire; the diminutive Wellchen is the joke, six full-grown trees called a little bundle. heimbringen is separable, and the particle stays put here only because the verb is in the infinitive.

sentences.t: Dann kam er wieder, und gieng mit seinem Herrn, der sprach „wir zwei sollten wohl durch die ganze Welt kommen.“
sentences.l: Then he came back, and went with his master, who said “we two should surely get through the whole world.”
sentences.i: Then he came back and went along with his master, who said, “We two should be able to get right through the world.”
sentences.n: “durch die ganze Welt kommen” — to get through the whole world, i.e. to make our way anywhere at all. It is the tale’s refrain and its title; it comes back with each new man.

sentences.t: Und als sie ein Weilchen gegangen waren, fanden sie einen Jäger, der lag auf den Knien, hatte die Büchse angelegt und zielte.
sentences.l: And when they had gone a little while, they found a huntsman who lay on his knees, had levelled his gun and was aiming.
sentences.i: And when they had gone a little way, they found a huntsman kneeling, his gun levelled, taking aim.

sentences.t: Sprach der Herr zu ihm „Jäger, was willst du schießen?“
sentences.l: Said the master to him “huntsman, what do you want to shoot?”

sentences.t: Er antwortete „zwei Meilen von hier sitzt eine Fliege auf dem Ast eines Eichbaums, der will ich das linke Auge heraus schießen.“
sentences.l: He answered “two miles from here a fly is sitting on the branch of an oak tree; to it I want to shoot out the left eye.”
sentences.i: He answered, “Two miles from here a fly is sitting on the branch of an oak, and I mean to shoot out its left eye.”
sentences.n: der… das linke Auge is the possessive dative — “to it the left eye,” where English says “its left eye”; the same construction as “he looked him in the eye.” A German Meile was far longer than an English mile, some seven kilometres, which makes the boast larger still.

sentences.t: „O, geh mit mir,“ sprach der Mann, „wenn wir drei zusammen sind, sollten wir wohl durch die ganze Welt kommen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, come with me,” said the man, “when we three are together, we should surely get through the whole world.”

sentences.t: Der Jäger war bereit und gieng mit ihm, und sie kamen zu sieben Windmühlen, deren Flügel trieben ganz hastig herum, und gieng doch links und rechts kein Wind, und bewegte sich kein Blättchen.
sentences.l: The huntsman was willing and went with him, and they came to seven windmills whose sails were driving round quite hastily, and yet there went no wind left or right, and no little-leaf moved.
sentences.i: The huntsman was ready enough and went with him, and they came to seven windmills whose sails were whirling round in great haste — and yet there was no wind on either side, and not a leaf was stirring.
sentences.n: Flügel are wings, and so also the sails of a mill. The sentence changes footing halfway: gieng doch… kein Wind puts the verb first because the clause carries on from the und, a looser join than modern German allows.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Mann „ich weiß nicht, was die Windmühlen treibt, es regt sich ja kein Lüftchen,“
sentences.l: Then said the man “I do not know what drives the windmills, there is not a breath of air stirring,”
sentences.i: Then said the man, “I cannot tell what is driving these windmills; there is not a breath of air stirring,”

sentences.t: und gieng mit seinen Dienern weiter, und als sie zwei Meilen fortgegangen waren, sahen sie einen auf einem Baum sitzen, der hielt das eine Nasenloch zu und blies aus dem andern.
sentences.l: and went on further with his servants, and when they had gone two miles, they saw one sitting on a tree who held the one nostril shut and blew out of the other.
sentences.i: and went on with his servants; and when they had gone two miles, they saw a man sitting in a tree who held one nostril shut and blew out of the other.

sentences.t: „Mein, was treibst du da oben?“ fragte der Mann.
sentences.l: “My, what are you doing up there?” asked the man.
sentences.i: “Well now, what are you about up there?” asked the man.
sentences.n: Mein! is an old exclamation of surprise, a clipped mein Gott — nearer to “goodness” than to anything possessive. treiben, used of the windmills two sentences ago (was die Windmühlen treibt), comes back here for what the man is doing: the tale names the answer before it is given.

sentences.t: Er antwortete „zwei Meilen von hier stehen sieben Windmühlen, seht, die blase ich an, daß sie laufen.“
sentences.l: He answered “two miles from here stand seven windmills; look, at those I am blowing, so that they run.”
sentences.i: He answered, “Two miles from here stand seven windmills; look — I am blowing on them to keep them turning.”

sentences.t: „O, geh mit mir,“ sprach der Mann, „wenn wir vier zusammen sind, sollten wir wohl durch die ganze Welt kommen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, come with me,” said the man, “when we four are together, we should surely get through the whole world.”

sentences.t: Da stieg der Bläser herab und gieng mit, und über eine Zeit sahen sie einen, der stand da auf einem Bein, und hatte das andere abgeschnallt und neben sich gelegt.
sentences.l: Then the blower climbed down and went along, and after a time they saw one who stood there on one leg, and had unbuckled the other and laid it beside him.
sentences.i: Then the blower climbed down and came along; and after a while they saw a man standing on one leg, who had unbuckled the other and laid it down beside him.
sentences.n: The tale gives no explanation at all — the leg simply unbuckles. abschnallen is what you do to a strap, and it is used again later when the leg goes back on.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Herr „du hast dirs ja bequem gemacht zum Ausruhen.“
sentences.l: Then said the master “you have indeed made it comfortable for yourself for resting.”
sentences.i: Then said the master, “You have certainly made yourself comfortable for a rest.”

sentences.t: „Ich bin ein Laufer,“ antwortete er, „und damit ich nicht gar zu schnell springe, habe ich mir das eine Bein abgeschnallt; wenn ich mit zwei Beinen laufe, so gehts geschwinder als ein Vogel fliegt.“
sentences.l: “I am a runner,” answered he, “and so that I do not spring far too fast, I have unbuckled the one leg; when I run with two legs, then it goes quicker than a bird flies.”
sentences.i: “I am a runner,” he answered, “and I have unbuckled one leg so as not to go far too fast; when I run on two legs it goes quicker than a bird flies.”
sentences.n: Laufer is the 1857 spelling of Läufer. A Läufer was also a great man’s running footman, who went ahead of the coach on foot — a real trade, which is part of why the tale can treat the gift so matter-of-factly.

sentences.t: „O, geh mit mir, wenn wir fünf zusammen sind, sollten wir wohl durch die ganze Welt kommen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, come with me; when we five are together, we should surely get through the whole world.”

sentences.t: Da gieng er mit, und gar nicht lang, so begegneten sie einem, der hatte ein Hütchen auf, hatte es aber ganz auf dem einen Ohr sitzen.
sentences.l: Then he went along, and not long at all, and they met one who had a little hat on, but had it sitting quite over on the one ear.
sentences.i: So he came along; and before very long they met a man with a little hat on, but wearing it cocked right over one ear.
sentences.n: “gar nicht lang, so…” — not long at all, and then: an old way of joining a stretch of time to what happened at the end of it, without a proper conjunction.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Herr zu ihm „manierlich! manierlich! häng deinen Hut doch nicht auf ein Ohr, du siehst ja aus wie ein Hans Narr.“
sentences.l: Then said the master to him “mannerly! mannerly! do not hang your hat on one ear like that, you look like a Hans Fool.”
sentences.i: Then said the master to him: “Manners, manners! Do not hang your hat over one ear so; you look like a jester.”
sentences.n: Hans Narr — “Hans the Fool,” the stock name for a clown, and the reason a jester’s cap sits crooked. manierlich is the adjective flung out on its own as a rebuke: decently! properly!

sentences.t: „Ich darfs nicht thun,“ sprach der andere, „denn setz ich meinen Hut gerad, so kommt ein gewaltiger Frost, und die Vögel unter dem Himmel erfrieren und fallen todt zur Erde.“
sentences.l: “I may not do it,” said the other, “for if I set my hat straight, then a mighty frost comes, and the birds under the heavens freeze and fall dead to the earth.”
sentences.i: “I dare not,” said the other, “for if I set my hat straight, a mighty frost comes on, and the birds under heaven freeze and fall dead to the ground.”
sentences.n: setz ich meinen Hut gerad is the verb-first conditional again. thun and todt are the 1857 spellings of tun and tot.

sentences.t: „O, geh mit mir,“ sprach der Herr, „wenn wir sechs zusammen sind, sollten wir wohl durch die ganze Welt kommen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, come with me,” said the master, “when we six are together, we should surely get through the whole world.”

sentences.t: Nun gingen die sechse in eine Stadt, wo der König hatte bekannt machen lassen wer mit seiner Tochter in die Wette laufen wollte, und den Sieg davon trüge, der sollte ihr Gemahl werden;
sentences.l: Now the six went into a town where the king had had it made known that whoever would run a race with his daughter, and carry off the victory, he should become her husband;
sentences.i: Now the six went into a town where the king had had it proclaimed that whoever would run a race against his daughter and carry off the victory should be her husband;
sentences.n: “in die Wette laufen” — to run for a wager, to race. The whole proclamation stands in the subjunctive (wollte, trüge, and verlöre, müßte in the next unit) because it is being reported rather than made. Note also gingen with the modern spelling here, where the tale writes gieng everywhere else: the 1857 edition is not perfectly consistent, and we keep what it prints.

sentences.t: wer aber verlöre, müßte auch seinen Kopf hergeben.
sentences.l: but whoever lost would also have to give up his head.
sentences.i: but whoever lost must forfeit his head into the bargain.

sentences.t: Da meldete sich der Mann, und sprach „ich will aber meinen Diener für mich laufen lassen.“
sentences.l: Then the man came forward and said “but I want to let my servant run for me.”
sentences.i: Then the man put himself forward and said, “But I mean to let my servant run for me.”
sentences.n: sich melden — to report oneself, to come forward as a candidate; still the word used for entering one’s name for anything.

sentences.t: Der König antwortete „dann mußt du auch noch dessen Leben zum Pfand setzen, also daß sein und dein Kopf für den Sieg haften.“
sentences.l: The king answered “then you must set his life in pledge as well, so that his head and yours both stand surety for the victory.”
sentences.i: The king answered, “Then you must set his life in pledge besides, so that his head and yours both answer for the victory.”
sentences.n: haften für is the language of debt and surety — to be liable for. The king turns a wager into a bond.

sentences.t: Als das verabredet und fest gemacht war, schnallte der Mann dem Laufer das andere Bein an und sprach zu ihm „nun sei hurtig und hilf daß wir siegen.“
sentences.l: When that was agreed and made fast, the man buckled the other leg on to the runner and said to him “now be quick and help that we win.”
sentences.i: When that was agreed and settled, the man buckled the other leg on to the runner and said to him, “Now be quick, and help us to the victory.”

sentences.t: Es war aber bestimmt, daß wer am ersten Wasser aus einem weit abgelegenen Brunnen brächte, der sollte Sieger sein.
sentences.l: But it had been laid down that whoever first brought water out of a far-off well, he should be the victor.
sentences.i: But it had been laid down that whichever of them first brought water from a distant well should be the winner.
sentences.n: am ersten for modern am ehesten/zuerst — soonest, first.

sentences.t: Nun bekam der Laufer einen Krug, und die Königstochter auch einen, und sie fiengen zu gleicher Zeit zu laufen an:
sentences.l: Now the runner got a jug, and the king’s-daughter one too, and they began to run at the same time:

sentences.t: aber in einem Augenblick, als die Königstochter erst eine kleine Strecke fort war, konnte den Laufer schon kein Zuschauer mehr sehen, und es war nicht anders, als wäre der Wind vorbei gesaust.
sentences.l: but in a moment, when the king’s-daughter was only a short stretch away, no onlooker could see the runner any more, and it was no otherwise than as if the wind had gone rushing past.
sentences.i: but in an instant, when the king’s daughter had gone only a short way, no onlooker could see the runner at all; it was for all the world as though the wind had gone rushing by.

sentences.t: In kurzer Zeit langte er bei dem Brunnen an, schöpfte den Krug voll Wasser und kehrte wieder um.
sentences.l: In a short time he arrived at the well, scooped the jug full of water and turned back again.

sentences.t: Mitten aber auf dem Heimweg überkam ihn eine Müdigkeit, da setzte er den Krug hin, legte sich nieder, und schlief ein.
sentences.l: But in the middle of the way home a weariness came over him; then he set the jug down, laid himself down, and fell asleep.

sentences.t: Er hatte aber einen Pferdeschädel, der da auf der Erde lag, zum Kopfkissen gemacht, damit er hart läge, und bald wieder erwachte.
sentences.l: But he had made a horse’s skull, which was lying there on the ground, into a pillow, so that he might lie hard and soon wake again.
sentences.i: But he had made a pillow of a horse’s skull that was lying there on the ground, so that he should lie hard and soon wake again.
sentences.n: läge is subjunctive, held by damit — the hard lying is the purpose, not yet a fact. The skull is the hinge of the whole race, and the tale drops it in as an afterthought.

sentences.t: Indessen war die Königstochter, die auch gut laufen konnte, so gut es ein gewöhnlicher Mensch vermag, bei dem Brunnen angelangt, und eilte mit ihrem Krug voll Wasser zurück;
sentences.l: Meanwhile the king’s-daughter, who could also run well — as well as an ordinary person is able — had arrived at the well, and hurried back with her jug full of water;
sentences.i: Meanwhile the king’s daughter, who could run well too, as well as an ordinary mortal can, had reached the well and was hurrying back with her jug full of water;

sentences.t: und als sie den Laufer da liegen und schlafen sah, war sie froh und sprach „der Feind ist in meine Hände gegeben,“ leerte seinen Krug aus und sprang weiter.
sentences.l: and when she saw the runner lying and sleeping there, she was glad and said “the enemy is given into my hands,” emptied out his jug and sprang onward.
sentences.i: and when she saw the runner lying asleep there, she was glad and said, “The enemy is delivered into my hands,” emptied out his jug and ran on.
sentences.n: She is not inventing the phrase: “der Feind ist in meine Hände gegeben” has the cadence of the Luther Bible, where a victory is spoken of as granted rather than won.

sentences.t: Nun wär alles verloren gewesen, wenn nicht zu gutem Glück der Jäger mit seinen scharfen Augen oben auf dem Schloß gestanden und alles mit angesehen hätte.
sentences.l: Now all would have been lost, if by good fortune the huntsman with his sharp eyes had not been standing up on the castle and watching it all.
sentences.i: Now all would have been lost, had not the huntsman with his sharp eyes been standing up on the castle by good fortune, watching the whole of it.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „die Königstochter soll doch gegen uns nicht aufkommen,“ lud seine Büchse und schoß so geschickt, daß er dem Laufer den Pferdeschädel unter dem Kopf wegschoß ohne ihm weh zu thun.
sentences.l: Then said he “the king’s-daughter shall not get the better of us after all,” loaded his gun and shot so skilfully that he shot the horse’s skull out from under the runner’s head without doing him harm.
sentences.i: Then said he, “The king’s daughter shall not get the better of us for all that,” loaded his gun, and shot so skilfully that he shot the horse’s skull out from under the runner’s head without hurting him.
sentences.n: gegen jemanden aufkommen — to come up against someone and prevail. dem Laufer… unter dem Kopf is the possessive dative once more: out from under his head.

sentences.t: Da erwachte der Laufer, sprang in die Höhe und sah daß sein Krug leer und die Königstochter schon weit voraus war.
sentences.l: Then the runner woke, sprang up into the height and saw that his jug was empty and the king’s daughter already far ahead.
sentences.i: Then the runner woke, sprang to his feet, and saw that his jug was empty and the king’s daughter already far ahead.

sentences.t: Aber er verlor den Muth nicht, lief mit dem Krug wieder zum Brunnen zurück, schöpfte aufs neue Wasser und war noch zehn Minuten eher als die Königstochter daheim.
sentences.l: But he did not lose courage, ran back with the jug to the well again, drew water anew and was home a full ten minutes sooner than the king’s daughter.
sentences.i: But he did not lose heart; he ran back to the well with the jug, drew water afresh, and was home a good ten minutes before the king’s daughter.

sentences.t: „Seht ihr,“ sprach er, „jetzt hab ich erst die Beine aufgehoben, vorher wars gar kein Laufen zu nennen.“
sentences.l: “Do you see,” said he, “only now have I picked up my legs; before that it was not to be called running at all.”
sentences.i: “You see,” said he, “it is only now that I have picked up my legs; what went before was not worth calling running.”

sentences.t: Den König aber kränkte es, und seine Tochter noch mehr, daß sie so ein gemeiner abgedankter Soldat davon tragen sollte;
sentences.l: But it galled the king, and his daughter still more, that so common a discharged soldier should carry her off;
sentences.n: gemein in 1857 still means common in rank — of the ranks, not of the officers — as much as it means base. abgedankt: paid off at the end of a war, as he was in the tale’s first sentence.

sentences.t: sie rathschlagten mit einander wie sie ihn sammt seinen Gesellen los würden.
sentences.l: they took counsel with one another how they might be rid of him together with his companions.
sentences.n: rathschlagen (modern ratschlagen) is built on Rath, the 1857 spelling of Rat, advice. sammt is the older samt, “together with.”

sentences.t: Da sprach der König zu ihr „ich habe ein Mittel gefunden, laß dir nicht bang sein, sie sollen nicht wieder heim kommen.“
sentences.l: Then said the king to her “I have found a means; do not let yourself be afraid, they shall not come home again.”
sentences.i: Then said the king to her: “I have found a way. Do not be uneasy; they shall never go home again.”
sentences.n: “laß dir nicht bang sein” — literally do not let it be anxious to you: the person stands in the dative and the fear is simply something that happens to her.

sentences.t: Und sprach zu ihnen „ihr sollt euch nun zusammen lustig machen, essen und trinken“ und führte sie zu einer Stube, die hatte einen Boden von Eisen, und die Thüren waren auch von Eisen, und die Fenster waren mit eisernen Stäben verwahrt.
sentences.l: And said to them “you shall now make merry together, eat and drink,” and led them to a room which had a floor of iron, and the doors were also of iron, and the windows were secured with iron bars.
sentences.i: And he said to them, “Now you shall make merry together, and eat and drink,” and led them to a room that had a floor of iron; and the doors were of iron too, and the windows were made fast with iron bars.

sentences.t: In der Stube war eine Tafel mit köstlichen Speisen besetzt, da sprach der König zu ihnen „geht hinein, und laßts euch wohl sein.“
sentences.l: In the room a table was set with costly dishes; then said the king to them “go in, and let it be well with you.”
sentences.i: In the room a table was spread with costly dishes, and the king said to them, “Go in, and enjoy yourselves.”
sentences.n: laßts is laßt es. “sich wohl sein lassen” — to let oneself be well, to make a good time of it; the king is being hospitable in exactly the words he needs for the trap.

sentences.t: Und wie sie darinnen waren, ließ er die Thüre verschließen und verriegeln.
sentences.l: And when they were inside, he had the door locked and bolted.

sentences.t: Dann ließ er den Koch kommen, und befahl ihm ein Feuer so lang unter die Stube zu machen, bis das Eisen glühend würde.
sentences.l: Then he had the cook come, and ordered him to make a fire under the room so long until the iron should be glowing.
sentences.i: Then he sent for the cook and ordered him to keep a fire under the room until the iron should be glowing.

sentences.t: Das that der Koch, und es fieng an und ward den sechsen in der Stube, während sie an der Tafel saßen, ganz warm, und sie meinten das käme vom Essen;
sentences.l: That the cook did, and it began, and it grew quite warm for the six in the room while they sat at the table, and they thought that came from the eating;
sentences.i: The cook did so; and it began, and the six in the room grew very warm as they sat at the table, and they supposed it came from the food;
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat. ward den sechsen… ganz warm puts the six in the dative — the warmth happens to them; German says “it grew warm to them” where English says “they grew warm.”

sentences.t: als aber die Hitze immer größer ward und sie hinaus wollten, Thüre und Fenster aber verschlossen fanden, da merkten sie daß der König Böses im Sinne gehabt hatte und sie ersticken wollte.
sentences.l: but when the heat grew greater and greater and they wanted out, but found door and windows locked, then they noticed that the king had had evil in mind and wanted to suffocate them.
sentences.i: but when the heat grew greater and greater and they wanted to get out, and found door and windows locked, then they saw that the king had meant them harm and would suffocate them.

sentences.t: „Es soll ihm aber nicht gelingen,“ sprach der mit dem Hütchen, „ich will einen Frost kommen lassen, vor dem sich das Feuer schämen und verkriechen soll.“
sentences.l: “But it shall not succeed for him,” said the one with the little hat, “I will let a frost come before which the fire shall be ashamed and crawl away.”
sentences.i: “But he shall not succeed,” said the one with the little hat; “I shall bring on a frost that will make the fire ashamed and send it creeping into a corner.”
sentences.n: gelingen puts the person in the dative and the undertaking in the nominative: the thing succeeds to him. The image of a fire ashamed of itself and crawling off to hide is the tale’s, not ours.

sentences.t: Da setzte er sein Hütchen gerade, und alsobald fiel ein Frost daß alle Hitze verschwand und die Speisen auf den Schüsseln anfiengen zu frieren.
sentences.l: Then he set his little hat straight, and at once such a frost fell that all the heat vanished and the food on the platters began to freeze.
sentences.n: alsobald — an older sofort/sogleich, at once.

sentences.t: Als nun ein paar Stunden herum waren, und der König glaubte sie wären in der Hitze verschmachtet, ließ er die Thüre öffnen und wollte selbst nach ihnen sehen.
sentences.l: When now a couple of hours were round, and the king believed they had perished in the heat, he had the door opened and wanted to look in on them himself.
sentences.i: When a couple of hours had gone round and the king believed they had perished in the heat, he had the door opened and would go and look at them himself.

sentences.t: Aber wie die Thüre aufgieng, standen sie alle sechse da, frisch und gesund, und sagten es wäre ihnen lieb daß sie heraus könnten, sich zu wärmen, denn bei der großen Kälte in der Stube frören die Speisen an den Schüsseln fest.
sentences.l: But as the door went open, there they all six stood, fresh and sound, and said it would be welcome to them that they could get out to warm themselves, for in the great cold in the room the food was freezing fast to the platters.
sentences.i: But when the door swung open, there they all six stood, fresh and well, and said they were glad to be let out to warm themselves, for in the great cold of that room the food was freezing fast to the platters.
sentences.n: wäre and frören are subjunctive because we are being told what they said. frören goes with the plural die Speisen; it is the ordinary subjunctive of frieren, not an old form.

sentences.t: Da gieng der König voll Zorn hinab zu dem Koch, schalt ihn und fragte warum er nicht gethan hätte was ihm wäre befohlen worden.
sentences.l: Then the king went down full of anger to the cook, scolded him and asked why he had not done what had been commanded him.
sentences.i: Then the king went down to the cook in a rage, scolded him, and asked why he had not done what he had been ordered.

sentences.t: Der Koch aber antwortete „es ist Glut genug da, seht nur selbst.“
sentences.l: But the cook answered “there is heat enough there, only look yourself.”
sentences.i: But the cook answered, “There is fire enough there — look for yourself.”
sentences.n: Glut is not flame but the red heat of the coals; a stronger word than Feuer for what is under the floor.

sentences.t: Da sah der König daß ein gewaltiges Feuer unter der Eisenstube brannte, und merkte daß er den sechsen auf diese Weise nichts anhaben könnte.
sentences.l: Then the king saw that a mighty fire was burning under the iron room, and noticed that he could do the six no harm in this way.
sentences.i: Then the king saw that a mighty fire was burning under the iron room, and understood that he could do the six no harm by this means.
sentences.n: “einem etwas anhaben” — to do someone harm; it survives almost only in the negative, as here.

sentences.t: Nun sann der König aufs neue wie er der bösen Gäste los würde, ließ den Meister kommen und sprach „willst du Gold nehmen, und dein Recht auf meine Tochter aufgeben, so sollst du haben so viel du willst.“
sentences.l: Now the king pondered anew how he might be rid of the wicked guests, had the master come and said “if you will take gold, and give up your right to my daughter, then you shall have as much as you want.”
sentences.i: Now the king cast about afresh for a way to be rid of these troublesome guests; he sent for the master and said, “If you will take gold and give up your claim to my daughter, you shall have as much as you please.”
sentences.n: der bösen Gäste los würde — loswerden with the genitive, an older government; modern German would say die Gäste loswerden. der Meister here is simply the master of the other five, the man of the first sentence.

sentences.t: „O ja, Herr König,“ antwortete er, „gebt mir so viel als mein Diener tragen kann, so verlange ich eure Tochter nicht.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes, my lord king,” answered he, “give me as much as my servant can carry, and then I do not ask for your daughter.”

sentences.t: Das war der König zufrieden, und jener sprach weiter „so will ich in vierzehn Tagen kommen und es holen.“
sentences.l: With that the king was content, and the other said further “then I will come in fourteen days and fetch it.”
sentences.i: With that the king was content, and the other went on, “Then I will come in a fortnight and fetch it.”
sentences.n: vierzehn Tage is the German for a fortnight — German counts the days where English counts the nights. jener, “that one,” points back to the further of the two men named, the master rather than the king.

sentences.t: Darauf rief er alle Schneider aus dem ganzen Reich herbei, die mußten vierzehn Tage lang sitzen und einen Sack nähen.
sentences.l: Thereupon he called together all the tailors out of the whole kingdom; those had to sit for fourteen days and sew a sack.

sentences.t: Und als er fertig war, mußte der Starke, welcher Bäume ausrupfen konnte, den Sack auf die Schulter nehmen und mit ihm zu dem König gehen.
sentences.l: And when it was finished, the strong one, who could pluck up trees, had to take the sack on his shoulder and go with it to the king.

sentences.t: Da sprach der König „was ist das für ein gewaltiger Kerl, der den hausgroßen Ballen Leinewand auf der Schulter trägt?“ erschrack und dachte „was wird der für Gold wegschleppen!“
sentences.l: Then said the king “what sort of a mighty fellow is that, who carries the house-big bale of linen on his shoulder?” and took fright and thought “what a quantity of gold that one will drag away!”
sentences.i: Then said the king, “What manner of giant fellow is this, who carries a bale of linen the size of a house on his shoulder?” — and he took fright and thought, “What a quantity of gold that man will haul away!”
sentences.n: erschrack is the 1857 spelling of erschrak. Leinewand (modern Leinwand) is plain linen cloth — the king still thinks he is looking at cloth, not at a sack.

sentences.t: Da hieß er eine Tonne Gold herbringen, die mußten sechzehn der stärksten Männer tragen, aber der Starke packte sie mit einer Hand, steckte sie in den Sack und sprach „warum bringt ihr nicht gleich mehr, das deckt ja kaum den Boden.“
sentences.l: Then he ordered a tun of gold to be brought; that took sixteen of the strongest men to carry, but the strong one seized it with one hand, stuck it into the sack and said “why do you not bring more at once, that hardly covers the bottom.”
sentences.i: Then he ordered a tun of gold to be brought, which sixteen of the strongest men had to carry; but the strong one took it up in one hand, thrust it into the sack, and said, “Why not bring more at once? That scarcely covers the bottom.”
sentences.n: eine Tonne Gold is a barrel of gold, and also a set expression for an enormous sum — a hundred thousand thalers. The tale means both.

sentences.t: Da ließ der König nach und nach seinen ganzen Schatz herbeitragen, den schob der Starke in den Sack hinein, und der Sack ward davon noch nicht zur Hälfte voll.
sentences.l: Then the king had his whole treasure carried up little by little; the strong one shoved it into the sack, and the sack was not yet half full from it.

sentences.t: „Schafft mehr herbei,“ rief er, „die paar Brocken füllen nicht.“
sentences.l: “Bring more here,” he called, “these few crumbs do not fill it.”
sentences.i: “Fetch more,” he called; “these few crumbs will not fill it.”

sentences.t: Da mußten noch siebentausend Wagen mit Gold in dem ganzen Reich zusammen gefahren werden: die schob der Starke sammt den vorgespannten Ochsen in seinen Sack.
sentences.l: Then seven thousand more wagons of gold had to be driven together from the whole kingdom: those the strong one shoved into his sack, together with the oxen harnessed in front of them.
sentences.i: Then seven thousand wagon-loads of gold more had to be brought together out of the whole kingdom, and the strong one shoved them into his sack, oxen and harness and all.

sentences.t: „Ich wills nicht lange besehen,“ sprach er, „und nehmen was kommt, damit der Sack nur voll wird.“
sentences.l: “I will not look at it long,” said he, “and take what comes, only so that the sack gets full.”
sentences.i: “I shall not stop to look it over,” said he, “but take whatever comes, so long as the sack gets full.”

sentences.t: Wie alles darin stack, gieng doch noch viel hinein, da sprach er „ich will dem Ding nur ein Ende machen, man bindet wohl einmal einen Sack zu, wenn er auch noch nicht voll ist.“
sentences.l: When everything was stuck in there, much more still went in; then he said “I will just make an end of the thing; one does tie up a sack sometimes, even when it is not yet full.”
sentences.i: When everything was in, there was still room for much more, and then he said, “I will simply make an end of it; a man does tie up his sack at some point, even if it is not yet full.”
sentences.n: stack is the old past of stecken (modern steckte or stak). The closing line has the shape of a proverb, though it is invented on the spot: the sack is never going to be full, so he stops.

sentences.t: Dann huckte er ihn auf den Rücken und gieng mit seinen Gesellen fort.
sentences.l: Then he humped it onto his back and went off with his companions.
sentences.n: hucken is a regional word for hoisting a load onto the back; it survives in Huckepack, a piggyback ride.

sentences.t: Als der König nun sah wie der einzige Mann des ganzen Landes Reichthum forttrug, ward er zornig und ließ seine Reiterei aufsitzen, die sollten den sechsen nachjagen, und hatten Befehl dem Starken den Sack wieder abzunehmen.
sentences.l: When the king now saw how the single man carried off the whole land’s wealth, he grew angry and had his cavalry mount; they were to chase after the six, and had orders to take the sack from the strong one again.
sentences.i: When the king saw how a single man was carrying off the wealth of the whole land, he grew angry and had his cavalry mount, to give chase to the six with orders to take the sack from the strong one again.
sentences.n: Reichthum is the 1857 spelling of Reichtum. aufsitzen of cavalry is to mount.

sentences.t: Zwei Regimenter holten sie bald ein, und riefen ihnen zu „ihr seid Gefangene, legt den Sack mit dem Gold nieder, oder ihr werdet zusammengehauen.“
sentences.l: Two regiments soon caught them up, and called to them “you are prisoners, lay down the sack with the gold, or you will be hewn to pieces.”
sentences.i: Two regiments soon overtook them and called out to them: “You are prisoners; lay down the sack of gold, or you will be cut to pieces.”

sentences.t: „Was sagt ihr?“ sprach der Bläser, „wir wären Gefangene? eher sollt ihr sämmtlich in der Luft herumtanzen,“
sentences.l: “What do you say?” said the blower, “that we are prisoners? sooner shall you all dance about in the air,”
sentences.i: “What is that you say?” said the blower. “We, prisoners? Sooner shall the lot of you go dancing about in the air,”
sentences.n: wären is subjunctive — he is holding their claim out at arm’s length, quoting it back rather than admitting it. sämmtlich is the 1857 spelling of sämtlich, the whole lot of you.

sentences.t: hielt das eine Nasenloch zu und blies mit dem andern die beiden Regimenter an, da fuhren sie aus einander und in die blaue Luft über alle Berge weg, der eine hierhin, der andere dorthin.
sentences.l: held the one nostril shut and blew at the two regiments with the other; then they flew apart and into the blue air away over all the mountains, the one this way, the other that.
sentences.i: and he held one nostril shut and blew on the two regiments with the other, so that they were scattered and carried off into the blue sky over all the hills, one man this way, another that.
sentences.n: “über alle Berge” — over all the hills — is the German for gone past recovery, the way English says “over the hills and far away.” Here the tale takes the idiom literally, which is exactly the joke.

sentences.t: Ein Feldwebel rief um Gnade, er hätte neun Wunden und wäre ein braver Kerl, der den Schimpf nicht verdiente.
sentences.l: A sergeant called for mercy: he had nine wounds and was a good fellow who did not deserve the disgrace.
sentences.i: A sergeant cried for mercy: he had nine wounds, he said, and was a good fellow who did not deserve such an indignity.
sentences.n: hätte and wäre mark the whole of it as the sergeant’s own plea reported. Schimpf is not injury but insult — being blown about the sky is beneath a soldier of nine wounds.

sentences.t: Da ließ der Bläser ein wenig nach, so daß er ohne Schaden wieder herab kam, dann sprach er zu ihm „nun geh heim zum König und sag er sollte nur noch mehr Reiterei schicken, ich wollte sie alle in die Luft blasen.“
sentences.l: Then the blower let up a little, so that he came down again without harm; then he said to him “now go home to the king and say he should just send still more cavalry, I would blow them all into the air.”
sentences.i: Then the blower eased off a little, so that the man came down again unhurt; and then he said to him: “Now go home to the king and tell him to send yet more cavalry — I would blow them all into the air.”

sentences.t: Der König, als er den Bescheid vernahm, sprach „laßt die Kerle gehen, die haben etwas an sich.“
sentences.l: The king, when he heard the answer, said “let the fellows go, they have something about them.”
sentences.i: The king, when he received the answer, said, “Let the fellows go; there is something about them.”
sentences.n: “die haben etwas an sich” — they have something about them: the king means something uncanny he cannot name, and it is his whole surrender.

sentences.t: Da brachten die sechs den Reichthum heim, theilten ihn unter sich und lebten vergnügt bis an ihr Ende.
sentences.l: Then the six brought the wealth home, divided it among themselves and lived contented until their end.
sentences.i: So the six brought the treasure home, shared it out among themselves, and lived contented to the end of their days.
sentences.n: theilten is the 1857 spelling of teilten. The soldier never does marry the princess, and the tale does not think this needs explaining: he came for the money.
